# Planning A New Data Context
## Simple Linear Regression Using the "cars" Data

Using R's built-in "cars" data, we will create a simple linear regression model.
The model will consist of miles-per-gallon (the response) and horsepower (the 
predictor). We will first use R's built-in summary() function so we can create
an estimated equation. Then, we will create a QQ-plot using the ggplot2 package 
to check the normality assumption of the model. 

# Simple Linear Regression Analysis

## Summary Output for Miles-Per-Gallon ~ Horsepower SLR

``` {r}
#| label: tbl-slrSummary
#| tbl-cap: "Miles-Per-Gallon ~ Horsepower: SLR Summary Output"
#| tbl-pos: "H"
#| tbl-width: 6.5
#| tbl-height: 3
#| tbl-alt: "A table featuring summary statistics of the mpg~hp SLR model"
#| echo: FALSE
data(mtcars)

carsModel <- lm(mpg ~ hp, data = mtcars)
summary(carsModel)
```

Using this table, we find that the estimated model is $\hat{Y} = 30.09886 - 0.06823X$. 
We also observe that the percentage of variability explained by the predictor (horsepower)
is 60.24%. If we wanted to test whether the true slope ($\beta_1$) for our model is 0, 
we could use the F-test statistic found at the bottom of @tbl-slrSummary, which is 45.46. 
Judging by the low p-value, for a 0.05 significance level,
we would reject the null hypothesis for this test. In other words, we could state with 
95% confidence that the slope ($\beta_1$) is not 0. 

## QQ-Plot for Miles-Per-Gallon ~ Horsepower SLR

``` {r}
#| label: fig-slrQQPlot
#| fig-cap: "QQ-Plot of Miles-Per-Gallon ~ Horsepower SLR Model"
#| fig-pos: "H"
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-alt: "A graph of sample quartiles versus theoretical quartiles of the SLR model"
#| echo: FALSE

data(mtcars)
#install.packages("ggplot2")
# un-comment above line if ggplot2 is not installed, then re-comment
library(ggplot2)

carsResiduals <- data.frame(residuals = resid(carsModel))

ggplot(data = carsResiduals, aes(sample = residuals)) +
  geom_qq()+
  geom_qq(color = "blue") +
  geom_qq_line() +
  labs(
    title = "QQ-Plot of Residuals",
    x = "Theoretical Quantiles",
    y = "Sample Quantiles",
  )

```

We observe a linear pattern in the QQ-plot. This suggests that the normality
assumption of our SLR model is met. There is a noticeably heavy right tail present 
in @fig-slrQQPlot, however this does not likely impede on our assumption, given that 
the overall pattern appears linear, and thus the errors are more than likely normal. 

# Course Reflection

In STAT 184, we began by installing R and RStudio. Before learning how to
write programs, we first had to gain proficiency in the skill of proper goal-setting
and planning. Then we applied these skills by creating simple functions in R (such as 
the die-rolling simulator and the restaurant selector). In unit 2, we were exposed
to the concept of a tidy data set (one consisting of cases as rows, and case attributes
as columns). We applied this notion through the use of functions from R and the tidyverse
package to clean-up data and make it tidy for later use.

With the ability to tidy data, we then learned how to make data visualizations such as
summary tables (like for the diamonds data in HW #3.1 and #3.3), as well as graphs using
ggplot2. At this point, we learned about the various geometries available for use in 
data visualizations, as well as strategies for creating effective plots for potential 
viewers.

This current unit has us using Quarto to create professional documents with text and figures. 
This may help us in the future when we need to create reports or analyses involving graphs we
have generated (perhaps with tidy data and using ggplot2), as well as narrative text to explain
any relevant statistical phenomenon.
